rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and definition conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of mathematical terms are given within paragraphs of text, rather than displayed separately like theorems. These definitions are indicated by the use of boldface type for the more important terms, with italics being used for less important or less formal definitions as well as for simple emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms defined using boldface appear in the Index, with the page number where the definition occurs listed first. Readers should look for boldface/italics to identify formal vs informal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the proof method with one’s own methods (Strategy 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the technique used in the proof with how you would have approached the problem to identify novel or useful methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes the method itself an explicit object of discussion, helps learners acquire new techniques, and aids transfer to future problems. Transcript evidence shows this fosters appreciation of novel techniques; survey support was high (≈86.7% preferred). Use this strategy to catalog useful ideas and to reflect on when alternative approaches might be advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feferman-style abstraction/generalization justification
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument for belief in certain mathematical entities: (1) scattered results call for explanation; (2) explanation is obtained by appealing to more abstract entities (ideals, analytic functions); (3) this gives reason to postulate those abstract entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this schema to evaluate internal mathematical cases where invoking abstract structures yields unifying/simplifying explanations of disparate data; examine whether such abstraction increases understanding enough to warrant ontological commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for computer-assisted proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation criteria for computer proofs focus on reliability, the level of conceptual development achieved, and the provision of understanding beyond mere verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer proofs are typically strong at checking low-level combinatorial cases but weaker at producing deep conceptual explanations or linking disparate fields. Philosophical concerns include assessing the reliability of automated inference, whether such proofs can yield a priori knowledge, and what counts as acceptable explanation. Debates consider whether additional standards (e.g., reproducibility, human-checkable high-level explanations) should be required for acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret and use previous theorems and definitions correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must use relevant theorems/definitions correctly and verify that the hypotheses/conditions of those theorems are satisfied before applying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common errors include ignoring relevant hypotheses, applying converses that do not hold, treating named theorems as vague 'slogans', and incorrect substitutions (especially for compound variables). Instruction should emphasise checking applicability and precise substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place your results in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how your work fits with, diverges from, and contributes to prior approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight novel contributions and the broader landscape. Use MathSciNet and Google Scholar to find related work; be generous in citing related articles to help readers situate your results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifying computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify computations step by step for the highest degree of trust; where needed, extract verified code for performance. The system should let users reason about results of computation within a precise formal semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional notation (mathematical symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and correctness of conventional mathematical notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded per segment (P/NP). Indicates teacher's attention to symbol use and conventional representation; part of 'knowledge of mathematical terrain' coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate proofs for elegance: conciseness, insightful steps, clever ideas, and avoidance of unnecessary technical baggage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance is context-dependent; prefer simpler, more illuminating arguments when they do not sacrifice necessary rigor or completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveals the 'why' (explanatory depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful mathematical argument 'helps the reader to understand why this piece of mathematics works this way, not just that it does.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable solutions expose the underlying ideas and mechanisms. Example: the triangular-number proof that pairs two triangles into a rectangle shows why the formula (n(n+1)/2) holds, not just that it does. This explanatory quality is 'critical' for mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressing dimensions and pictures (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing three-dimensional geometric intuition with n-dimensional formal manipulations from the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid starting with high-dimensional formal generalizations that remove the original geometric picture; preserve and communicate dimensional intuition where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the role and meaning of examples and counterexamples in forming conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sequences of examples and search for counterexamples to delimit the scope of empirical observations and to motivate precise conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate with the example about partitions of consecutive odd numbers where a simple pattern breaks (1,2,4,8,16, then 29) to show the need for counterexamples in hypothesis formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases as a general technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the proof into exhaustive cases covering all possibilities and prove the goal in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Proof Designer, selecting a disjunction given and giving the Cases command will create case subproofs; you can also supply a distinguishing predicate as a case split for a goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and description of proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The various techniques used in virtually all proofs, independent of subject matter, are identified and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 1 of the book catalogs techniques used in proofs so students can learn a toolbox of methods applicable across subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical philosophy: emphasis on intuitive understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should prioritize intuitive, meaningful formulas and arguments rather than producing results by any means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanley discusses when an answer is a 'good' answer and what should be considered a 'combinatorial' argument; the approach emphasizes that 'wherever possible the terms of the resulting formula should have intuitive meaning' and favors intuitive understanding over merely establishing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide examples of elegant proofs and curated resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Show students examples of elegant proofs and point them to textbooks and collections of elegant proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resources such as Proofs from THE BOOK, Charming Proofs, HOW TO THINK LIKE A MATHEMATICIAN, and other listed texts; present model 'elegant' proofs (e.g., the pigeonhole principle example) to illustrate style and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs as clear and simple as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful proofs that will stand up to scrutiny are important; proofs should be written to make any weaknesses easy to detect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not weaken standards of proof, but emphasize clarity and simplicity so that errors are visible and fixable; supply details where needed and avoid unnecessary formal complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: shows the underlying picture, not just the formal argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides heuristic explanations, mental models, or cartoons that help users grasp why results are true and how to generalize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof scheme appropriate for existence theorems where the student constructs an example or object to demonstrate existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By definition applies to existence proofs; combinatorial binomial identities are not existence statements, so this scheme was unlikely and not observed in the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation elegance and usability
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance and efficiency of the symbolic or notational system used to express mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses Arabic numerals as an example of a 'beautiful idea' because the notation is elegant, efficient and gives 'instant understanding' by length. Guidance: notation that reduces cognitive load and clarifies structure is aesthetically valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize human-understandable proofs (while maintaining standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be clear, simple, and humanly understandable; formal completeness is a different and complementary aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect careful proofs that will stand scrutiny, but value clarity that makes potential weaknesses easy to detect. Do not conflate human-checkable arguments with lax standards; rather, make arguments explicit enough for critical examination. Formal, fully machine-checked proofs are desirable but currently often impractical for entire bodies of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of diagrams/intuitions in geometric proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric proofs involve an indispensable diagrammatic role for intuitions; intuitions exhibit relations used in proofs and infer universal rules from singular displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drawing a pair of intersecting chords in a circle and inferring the universal relation; debates exist whether such intuitions function phenomenologically (immediacy) or logically (singularity/instantiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the epistemic role of computer proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze why computer-assisted or computer-generated proofs may fail to provide the sort of understanding mathematicians seek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish verification from understanding; address limits of computer proofs regarding explanation, insight, and fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use a repertoire of examples, counterexamples, non-examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A rich concept image (many varied examples and near-examples) supports flexible use of concepts in proofs and in judging conjectures; one counterexample can disprove a conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage generation of examples (not only memorisation). Pedagogically useful examples are 'only just' examples; useful non-examples are 'very nearly' examples. Beware students' reluctance to generate diverse examples or tendency to re-use a single prototypical example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs checkable from the axioms alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be verifiable by a reader who knows only the axioms, not the author's intended interpretation or motivating intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The axiomatic method 'provides clarity and rigor'—readers should be able to follow and validate the reasoning starting from the stated axioms. Avoid appeals to unformalized intuition or domain‑specific heuristics that are not derivable from axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the method, not merely the truth of theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not concerned about the truth of your Theorems, but only about the way of coming at them; whether it be legitimate or illegitimate, clear or obscure, scientific or tentative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging mathematical work, focus on the legitimacy, clarity, and scientific status of the method used to obtain results rather than only on whether the final results happen to be correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of insight (one key idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof turns on one key idea that, once seen, illuminates the result completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key idea should be extractable and expressible succinctly; it should explain why the theorem is true rather than merely verifying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses stated before theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hypotheses to theorems are stated a bit before the theorems rather than in the theorems themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: check surrounding text for assumptions that are not repeated in the theorem statement itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest and accurate claims of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author claims that a result is more general than earlier work, that claim should be supported by the actual scope of hypotheses and proofs; overstatement of generality is a methodological flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Hahn's tendency to insist on generality and simplicity even when results were not as general as claimed. Evaluate claims by checking whether the stated hypotheses truly cover the asserted breadth; prefer transparent definitions and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites (2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining and stating what background the reader needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State assumed knowledge explicitly to set reader expectations; avoid unnecessary prerequisites; indicate references for background material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using an example to understand a confusing inference
rubrics_metrics.description: When puzzled by a general assertion in a proof, instantiate it with a concrete numerical or specific example to see what the assertion is claiming and why it holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: helps interpret general statements and clarify the meaning of assertions (e.g., divisibility statements). Example transcript: to understand 'if d is a divisor of n then n/d is also a divisor of n', a student used 7 and 21 to see the partner factor 3. Survey evidence: 77% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 43% of mathematics majors reported using it. Anti-pattern: insisting one must only follow formal derivations and refusing to check plausibility by example; note that examples do not prove the statement but can aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical writing and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for writing proofs: clarity, correct notation, logical flow, and sufficient explanation so readers can follow each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contains a dedicated section (5.3) on mathematical writing: use clear definitions, state hypotheses, avoid ambiguous notation, and present proofs in readable steps. Exercises and examples illustrate good vs poor practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Clear and correct mathematical arguments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write arguments so that each step and the overall structure are easy to follow; clarity includes correct notation, explicit hypotheses, and readable exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of individual steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Each step in a proof requires separate justification based on the concepts involved; steps should not be left as unjustified leaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that claims labelled as 'Step (1)', 'Step (2)', etc., are supported by arguments or references. The text uses Lagrange's theorem to illustrate that stepwise justification (e.g., disjointness of cosets, cardinality claims, existence of representatives) is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and comprehensibility of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should avoid an impenetrable style — definitions, theorems, and proofs must be presented so that experts outside the author's immediate circle can follow the ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes long definitions followed by very short proofs and 'vast fields of trivialities followed by an enormous cliff of unjustified conclusions.' Good exposition means making the key ideas accessible and avoid producing a 'cloud of fog' for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas and display equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid built-up fractions and other complicated equation structures in text; put complicated expressions as display equations centered on their own line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display equations are usually numbered consecutively to facilitate citation in text (equation number in parentheses set flush right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision (define terms and quantify symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every mathematical statement has a precise meaning: define terms, use symbols consistently, and quantify every symbolic name appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What does it mean?' (make terms/symbols defined before first use) and 'Why is it true?' (justify statements by axiom, theorem, definition, hypothesis, a previous step, or logic). Cite reasons when helpful; sometimes obvious steps may be left unstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how previous results can be used
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking a theorem, state the theorem and explain how its hypotheses are satisfied before applying its conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'According to Theorem 20, every nonconstant linear function is a bijection. Consequently, because both f and g are nonconstant linear functions, they are injective and surjective. Then, by Theorem 21 (composition of injective functions is injective), since f and g are both injective, f∘g is injective.' Explicitly connect hypotheses to the current situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions: add value beyond summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a conclusions section that merely repeats the introduction. Instead, emphasize key ideas from the body that were hard to explain earlier and discuss conjectures, open problems, and plausible extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conclusions to suggest directions beyond the paper rather than duplicate content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design proof-state and method models for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a notion of proof state (local knowledge and subgoals) and treat methods as algorithms transforming proof states; evaluate methods by how they reduce epistemic requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A syntactic representation of proof states and algorithmic methods enables concrete evaluation of effectiveness, generality, and applicability; avoid overspecific representations but capture enough detail to compare methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and symbolic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (or lack) of symbolic notation in algebraic work and the implications for clarity and generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Saracen algebraists, including Omar, used names rather than symbols (following Diophantos's practice). The essay contrasts this rhetorical notation with symbolic methods, implying that notation choice is a relevant evaluative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start proofs with a warm-up
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs have easy and hard parts, do the easier parts first to build intuition and momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warm-ups help readers understand techniques and prepare them for the harder steps, especially when parts share ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent proofs at an appropriate level of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The language and representation of proofs should allow conveying algebraic/group-theoretic reasoning succinctly and in a way that mirrors informal mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Isabelle examples show that with appropriate locale/module support and notation, one can express results like Euler's theorem via a short chain of interpreted lemmas and simple rewriting steps, matching informal higher-level proofs while remaining checkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Writing (exposition and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on writing clear mathematical proofs and exposition (section noted as 'Mathematical Writing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize clarity, use of definitions, logical order, proper notation, and concise presentation; the text includes exercises and 'Some Words of Advice' to improve exposition and avoid common stylistic mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grader expects justification for each inferential step; unstated or unjustified steps cause deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: Place your results in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how your work fits in with and diverges from previous approaches by highlighting novel contributions and illustrating the broader landscape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MathSciNet/Google Scholar to find related work; be generous in citing related articles to help readers situate your results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and highlight specific concerning steps
rubrics_metrics.description: There are still explicit concerns around one specific step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parts of an argument are suspect, point them out clearly and explain why they are problematic; flagging specific steps enables targeted scrutiny rather than blanket acceptance or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete examples and counterexamples to motivate assumptions and show why certain conditions are necessary (or overly restrictive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples clarify why assumptions exist and when results fail or can be relaxed.
